what_it_does: Training a neural network normally requires backpropagation — sending an error signal backward through every layer of the network to update every weight. This works well on powerful servers but is impractical on tiny devices like smartwatches or hearing aids: it requires storing all the intermediate activations (the outputs of each layer during the forward pass) in memory, which is prohibitive, and it demands that layers wait on each other in a lockstep chain. Bio-FO proposes a different training scheme where each layer trains independently using only a forward pass, never requiring backward signals to flow between layers, making it far more memory-efficient and hardware-friendly.
method_in_detail:
The idea. Standard backpropagation has four biologically and practically inconvenient properties: (1) weight transport — the backward pass needs the exact same weight matrices used in the forward pass, transposed; (2) non-locality — the error at layer 5 must reach all the way back to layer 1; (3) update locking — layer 1 cannot update until the full forward and backward passes finish; (4) frozen activities — the output of each layer must be kept in memory until the backward pass arrives. Bio-FO eliminates all four.

How it works. Each hidden layer l in the network is trained completely independently:

1. Forward pass through layer l computes an activation vector h_l from the previous layer's output.
2. A tiny fixed random matrix B_l (random numbers, never updated) projects h_l down to a class-prediction vector a_l. This replaces the need for a true backward path — there is no symmetry requirement because B_l is never learned.
3. A standard cross-entropy loss is computed between a_l and the true label. The gradient flows backward only through B_l to compute a correction for h_l, which then propagates back through layer l alone to update its weights.
4. Layer l's weights are immediately updated. No other layer is involved. No other layer's activations need to be stored.

A sparsity mask S_l can be applied to the weight matrix at each layer, enabling the same algorithm to work for locally connected (LC) networks and convolutional neural networks (CNNs) — where each unit only connects to nearby units — which is a more biologically realistic architecture.

The key design choice. Using a fixed random projection matrix B_l rather than a learned backward pathway avoids weight transport while still providing a useful error signal: it is mathematically an unbiased estimate of the true gradient direction. The 'local only' training rule means layers can update in parallel or on a rolling basis, using only the memory for one layer at a time.

The result. On an NVIDIA Jetson Nano (a small embedded AI board drawing 5–10 watts), Bio-FO uses about 3x less memory than backpropagation during training and consumes up to 19.8x less energy than the next-best forward-only algorithm (FF) on CIFAR-100, while achieving higher accuracy than all prior forward-only methods and coming within a few percent of full backpropagation accuracy.
